threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflow, main issues, and project scope before design work.

messages.text:
Kicking off the rollout of the new outpatient check-in and triage process for project_pack_ref: Rollout of New Outpatient Check-in and Triage Process.
To get started, can each of you describe how check-in and triage currently work in your shift or area, and the main pain points you see?
I will use your inputs to start T1 and a first draft of the workflow map in A1. It would help if you mention:
- steps from patient arrival to being seen by the nurse
- where delays usually happen
- any data or consent issues you notice
Thanks in advance for detailed notes so we can align scope and objectives.

From the front desk side in the morning shift:
- Patients usually queue at the reception window and we check them in one by one in the EHR.
- We ask for ID, verify insurance, and give them a paper form to fill in if they are new or if something changed.
- Once the form is back, we type the data into the system and then call the nurse station to let them know the patient is ready.
Pain points I see:
- Sometimes patients arrive all at once and the queue gets long.
- People often do not complete the paper form correctly, so we have to ask again.
- When it is busy, I sometimes forget to note special comments for the nurse.
Not sure if this is detailed enough for T1, but I can try to add more if needed.

From the nursing side:
- We usually get a call or a quick note from reception when a patient is checked in.
- I then open the EHR, review the reason for visit and any alerts, and call the patient from the waiting room.
- Basic triage is done in the exam room: vitals, brief history, and risk flags.
Pain points:
- Sometimes the reason for visit is missing or very vague, so I have to spend extra time clarifying.
- Consent status is not always obvious in the record when the patient is new or has not been here for a while.
- During peak hours, patients arrive faster than we can triage, so the waiting room fills up.
For A1 and T1, I suggest we explicitly map where information is captured on paper versus directly in the EHR, because that is where we see inconsistencies.

From a quality perspective, based on spot checks:
- The sequence you both described matches what I have seen on site.
- There is variation between early morning and late afternoon: in the afternoon, some staff skip double-checking contact details to speed things up.
- I have noticed discrepancies between paper forms and what ends up in the EHR, especially around phone numbers and allergies.
For T1 and later T4, it would be useful if we capture:
- where checks are supposed to happen versus where they actually happen
- which steps are critical for safety (e.g. allergy information) versus administrative.
This will help us later when we design the QC checklist and link it back to A1.

Adding from my experience covering late shifts at reception:
- We often have fewer staff, so one person does check-in, phone calls, and printing forms.
- If a patient has been here recently, we usually just ask if anything changed and skip giving the full form again.
- For walk-ins, we sometimes do a quick registration and let the nurse complete details later.
Pain points:
- It is easy to miss fields when we are multitasking.
- We do not have a clear rule on when to reuse old forms versus asking for a new one.
This might be relevant for T1 and later T2 when we standardise the forms and rules.

From what I have observed when shadowing both reception and nursing for training preparation:
- There is no single visual overview of the process on the wall or in a shared folder, so new staff learn by asking colleagues.
- The same questions are sometimes asked twice: once on paper at reception and again verbally by the nurse.
- There is no simple checklist for staff to know if they have completed all steps for a patient.
For A1 and later training materials, I suggest we:
- create a clear step-by-step flow that can be used in induction
- highlight which steps are mandatory for compliance and which are optional.
This will also help when we define objectives and success metrics for the project.

Thanks for the detailed descriptions so far.
To move towards clear objectives for this rollout, can we align on:
1) What we want to improve most: waiting time, data quality, or something else?
2) How we will know it is working: for example, average time from arrival to triage, percentage of complete forms, number of incidents logged.
Please share your top 2 or 3 priorities. I will consolidate them into draft success metrics for D1 and link them to A1 and the incident log in A6 later on.

My top priorities:
1) Reduce time from arrival to first clinical contact, especially during peak hours.
2) Ensure that key clinical information (reason for visit, allergies, current medications) is complete and visible at triage.
3) Avoid missed or delayed escalations for urgent cases.
For metrics, I suggest:
- average and 90th percentile time from check-in to triage
- percentage of triage records with all key fields completed
- number of escalation-related incidents recorded in A6.
These could form the core of D1.

From a quality and audit angle, I would add:
- Reduce discrepancies between paper forms and EHR entries.
- Increase the proportion of check-ins that pass a basic QC check without corrections.
Possible metrics:
- percentage of records with no missing mandatory fields
- number of data correction incidents per week in A6
- sample-based error rate from the future QC checklist in A4.
Combining these with the timing metrics that 313168 suggested should give us a balanced view for D1.

From reception, my priorities are:
- Shorter queues at the desk, especially when phones are ringing.
- Clearer forms so patients do not leave fields blank or ask the same questions repeatedly.
- Fewer times we have to re-enter or correct data in the EHR.
Maybe we can track:
- average time spent per patient at the desk
- number of incomplete forms per shift
- number of times we have to call patients back to the desk because something is missing.

I agree with what others said. For me, the main thing is that the process is clear and simple to follow when it is busy.
I would like:
- a clear list of what I must always ask and record
- a way to avoid writing the same information twice.
I am not sure how to define metrics, but if we see fewer complaints at the desk and fewer calls from nurses asking for missing information, that would feel like success.

Thinking ahead to training and communication, I would add one more objective:
- Staff should be able to explain the new process clearly to patients in simple terms.
We could check this informally during training sessions and maybe through a short patient feedback question after go-live.
This is softer than the timing and data metrics, but it will influence patient experience and how well the new workflow is accepted.

Thanks all, this is very helpful. Let me summarise a draft for D1 so we can confirm or adjust:
Proposed main objectives for the new check-in and triage process:
1) Shorten and stabilise time from arrival to triage, especially during peak hours.
2) Improve completeness and consistency of key data in the EHR (reason for visit, contact details, allergies, consent).
3) Reduce rework at reception and in nursing (duplicate questions, corrections).
4) Support clear communication with patients about what to expect.
Proposed success metrics:
- average and 90th percentile time from check-in to triage
- percentage of records with all mandatory fields completed
- number of data correction and escalation incidents logged in A6
- qualitative feedback from staff and patients during pilot.
If there are no strong objections, I will record this as D1 and reflect it in A1 and later artifacts.

The summary for D1 looks good to me and covers both clinical and operational aspects.
One suggestion: when we define mandatory fields later for A2 and T2, we should align them directly with these metrics so that we do not add extra fields that slow things down without improving safety or data quality.

Agree with D1 as summarised.
For later QC work (A4, T4, T9), I will make sure the checklist and audit routine use the same metrics and mandatory fields so that we can track progress consistently from pilot to full rollout.

Next, we should clarify which parts of the current workflow must stay unchanged in the first rollout so we do not create disruption.
My initial thought for D2 is that we keep stable:
- appointment scheduling rules and time slots
- the core EHR registration screens (we only adjust the sequence and guidance, not the underlying system)
- existing clinical guidelines for treatment, outside of triage and escalation.
We would mainly change:
- the order and content of check-in questions
- the triage steps and documentation
- how we use paper versus electronic forms.
Please flag anything you believe must not change in this first phase, especially regarding regulations or system constraints.

From a clinical standpoint, I agree that we should not change underlying treatment guidelines or appointment scheduling rules in this rollout.
I would also keep unchanged:
- existing emergency response protocols and escalation outside the outpatient context
- how we document serious incidents in the broader clinical incident system.
Within triage, we can standardise categories and documentation as long as we align with current clinical guidance and get sign-off from the head nurse.

On the reception side, I think we should keep:
- the same opening hours and basic queue system
- the same way we verify identity and insurance, since that is tied to finance and policy.
I am comfortable changing the layout of the forms and the order of questions, as long as we still capture what finance and compliance need.

From quality and compliance:
- We must not weaken any existing data protection or consent requirements.
- Any new or revised forms in A2 must be reviewed with the appropriate compliance contact before use.
Within that boundary, we can simplify wording and layout.
I support the idea that we do not change the core EHR configuration in this phase; instead, T6 should focus on clarifying the sequence and responsibilities for data entry.

For training design, it helps if we can tell staff clearly what is changing and what is not.
Based on the discussion, I will draft a simple before and after slide using A1 that highlights:
- unchanged elements: appointment rules, emergency protocols, identity checks, core EHR screens
- changed elements: intake forms, triage documentation, order of steps.
Once we confirm D2, I will use that as the basis for T5.

Let me capture D2 based on the inputs:
For the first rollout, we will keep unchanged:
- appointment scheduling rules and time slots
- core EHR registration configuration
- identity and insurance verification steps
- existing emergency and serious incident protocols
- underlying clinical treatment guidelines.
We will focus changes on:
- standardising and simplifying intake and consent forms (A2, T2)
- defining a clear triage and escalation protocol (A3, T3)
- clarifying the sequence and responsibilities for data entry (T1, T6).
I will reflect this in the current vs future workflow map in A1.
If anyone sees a conflict with regulations or system constraints, please raise it, otherwise I will log this as D2.
This summary for D2 matches my understanding and is safe from a clinical perspective, provided we get the usual sign-off on the new triage protocol from the head nurse once T3 and A3 are drafted.

threads.thread_goal: Design and validate the new workflow, forms, and triage protocol.

messages.text:
Following up on D1 and D2, I have uploaded first drafts for:
- updated workflow map in A1 (current vs future)
- standardised intake and consent forms in A2 (two languages)
- a proposed data entry sequence aligned with the EHR for T6.
For T2, I tried to keep mandatory fields limited to what we need for safety, contact, billing, and consent.
Can you review and comment on:
1) Are any critical fields missing or unclear?
2) Are there fields we can remove or move to a later step to avoid slowing down check-in?
3) Does the future workflow in A1 reflect how you think it should work in practice?

I have reviewed the drafts in A1 and A2.
On the intake form (T2):
- The section on reason for visit is currently a free text box. I suggest adding a short list of common categories with checkboxes plus a free text field. This will help with triage and reporting.
- Allergies and current medications should be clearly marked as required for clinical safety.
- Consent wording looks generally fine, but we should have it checked by the compliance contact.
On the workflow in A1:
- The future flow correctly shows that basic demographics and consent are captured at reception, while detailed clinical history is captured during triage.
- I recommend adding an explicit step where the nurse confirms that consent is recorded before proceeding with any invasive procedure.
These points will also feed into T3 and A3 when we finalise the triage protocol.

From a quality and compliance angle, after a first pass on A2:
- Mandatory fields: I agree with making demographics, contact details, allergies, and consent mandatory. Insurance details can be mandatory for scheduled visits but optional for urgent walk-ins, to avoid delays.
- Data protection: we should add a short note on how data is stored and who can access it, in line with our existing privacy notice. I will check this with the compliance officer.
- Layout: grouping mandatory fields at the top of the form will help reception staff focus on what must be completed before triage.
For T6, the proposed EHR sequence looks reasonable, but we should test it with a couple of real cases to ensure there are no hidden dependencies in the system.

Looking at the new intake form in A2 from the reception side:
- The layout is clearer than the current one, especially the contact details section.
- I like that there is a separate area for emergency contact.
- One concern: the form is two pages now. When it is busy, patients sometimes miss the second page.
Could we either shorten it or make the second page clearly marked so people do not forget to turn over?

I checked the form too.
- The instructions at the top are helpful, but some patients may still ask for help with the consent section.
- The language level seems a bit formal in some parts.
If possible, I would appreciate a short guide or script so we know how to explain the key points in simple terms when patients ask.

Good point about the language.
For T5, I can draft a short explanation script and include it in the training materials, so reception and nursing staff have consistent wording when explaining consent and data use.
I can also review the text in A2 to simplify phrasing where possible, while keeping the legal meaning. I will coordinate with 437517 and the compliance contact on that.

On T3 and A3, I have drafted a triage protocol with three urgency levels plus a fast-track for very simple visits.
Key elements:
- Level 1: emergency, immediate nurse and physician review.
- Level 2: urgent, triage within 15 minutes.
- Level 3: routine, triage within 60 minutes.
- Fast-track: simple administrative or follow-up visits that can be handled quickly.
Escalation criteria include chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe pain, and other red flags.
Please review A3 and let me know if the categories and response times are realistic for our clinic, and if there are any conditions we should add or clarify.

Thanks for drafting A3.
From an operational view, the three levels plus fast-track make sense.
We should check how these map to the EHR fields in T6. For example:
- Do we have existing triage priority codes that match these levels, or do we need to adapt the wording?
- Can we add a simple drop-down for triage level so that we can later report on waiting times by level?
I will check the EHR configuration and propose a mapping in the T6 notes.

On A3, the structure looks aligned with common triage models.
For quality monitoring, I suggest we:
- define clear examples for each level to reduce variation between nurses
- specify how we will audit adherence to response times using A6.
We should also confirm with the head nurse that the proposed response times are feasible with current staffing before we finalise D4.

Agreed. I will add concrete examples to each triage level in A3 and then share the updated version with the head nurse for validation.
Once we have that sign-off, we can consider the protocol ready for D4.

To move towards D3 on the intake and consent forms, let me summarise the proposed structure for A2 based on feedback:
- Page 1: demographics, contact details, emergency contact, allergies, current medications, consent statement and signature.
- Page 2: reason for visit (with checkboxes plus free text), brief medical history, and optional additional information.
Mandatory fields before triage:
- name, date of birth, contact phone
- allergies, current medications
- consent signature (unless not applicable for the visit type, to be clarified with compliance).
We will:
- simplify language where possible
- clearly mark mandatory fields
- add a note on data protection and who can access the data.
If there are no major objections, I propose we treat this as the agreed structure for D3, subject to final compliance review.

This structure for A2 works for me.
Having all mandatory items on the first page will make it easier at the desk, and we can remind patients to complete page 2 while they wait if needed.

I am comfortable with this as the basis for D3, with the condition that we get written confirmation from the compliance officer on the consent and data protection wording.
Once that is done, I will note in our quality documentation that A2 is the approved standard form.

The head nurse has reviewed the updated A3 and agreed with the three levels plus fast-track and the proposed response times, with one clarification:
- Level 2 (urgent) triage within 30 minutes instead of 15, to match staffing reality.
I have updated A3 accordingly.
With this adjustment, I believe we can confirm D4, assuming no objections from the rest of you.

Thanks for securing that validation.
From the workflow and EHR side, the updated response times in A3 are feasible, and we can track them using timestamps in the system as part of T6 and A6.
I support confirming D4 with the revised Level 2 timing.

From a quality monitoring perspective, the adjusted Level 2 target is more realistic and will reduce the risk of constant breaches.
I will incorporate these response times into the future QC checklist in A4 and the pilot metrics in A6.
No objections to confirming D4.

threads.thread_goal: Define quality control approach and how audits and incidents will be handled.

messages.text:
I have drafted:
- a Daily Check-in and Triage Quality Control Checklist in A4 (for T4)
- an incident and improvement log template in A6 (for T12), which we can also use during the pilot.
The checklist covers key steps at reception and triage, including data completeness, consent, and triage level documentation.
The log template has fields for date, time, description, category, impact, and follow-up.
Please review and share feedback on:
1) Are we checking the right things daily, or is anything missing or unnecessary?
2) How often should we run audits per shift, and who should be responsible?
3) How should we categorise incidents and improvement suggestions in A6 so that we can review them efficiently?

Looking at A4 from the reception side:
- The items on identity verification, contact details, and consent are clear.
- There is a question about whether the intake form is fully completed and signed, which is useful.
One suggestion: could we add a simple yes or no item on whether the EHR record matches the paper form for a small sample of patients? That would help us catch data entry issues early.
On responsibilities, I think it would be practical if one person per shift is designated to complete the checklist, rotating among staff so it does not always fall on the same person.

From the nursing side, A4 covers the main clinical safety points:
- triage level recorded
- vital signs documented
- escalation criteria applied when needed.
I would add:
- a check that allergies and current medications are visible in the EHR at the time of triage
- a note on whether the triage level chosen matches the examples in A3, at least for a sample.
For A6, I suggest categories such as: data error, delay, escalation issue, patient complaint, and suggestion for improvement. This will make it easier to spot patterns during reviews.

For reception, the checklist looks manageable as long as it does not take too long.
If we do a small sample per shift, like 3 to 5 patients, I think it is realistic.
I like the idea of rotating who fills it in, but we should have clear instructions so everyone knows how to answer the questions consistently.

I agree with 438229 that clear instructions would help.
Sometimes checklists use terms that are not obvious when we are in a hurry.
Maybe we can have a short example or explanation for each item in A4, at least for the first weeks.

For T5 and training, I can include a short section on how to use A4 and A6, with examples of:
- what counts as a data error versus a delay
- how to write a clear incident description
- how to record suggestions for improvement.
This should help make the daily audits and logging more consistent across shifts.

Thanks for the feedback.
I will update A4 to:
- include a small sample check comparing paper forms and EHR entries
- add items on visibility of allergies and medications at triage
- provide brief guidance text for each checklist item.
For A6, I will add the categories suggested by 313168 and include a field for whether the entry is an incident or an improvement idea.
Next, we should agree on D5: daily audit routine, responsibilities, and minimum compliance threshold.
My proposal:
- One checklist per shift (morning, afternoon, evening), covering a sample of 5 patients.
- A designated person per shift, rotating weekly.
- Minimum compliance threshold: 90 percent of sampled records must meet all mandatory checks, with action required if we fall below this for more than two consecutive days.
Please share if this feels realistic or if we need to adjust the sample size or threshold.

From an operations point of view, one checklist per shift with 5 patients seems manageable.
The 90 percent threshold is ambitious but probably achievable once the new process stabilises.
I suggest that if we fall below the threshold, we:
- review the incidents in A6 for that period
- agree on one or two quick actions, such as a reminder in the next huddle or a small tweak to the workflow.
This will keep the audits focused on improvement rather than just measurement.

I am comfortable with the proposed routine and threshold for D5.
For nursing, we can integrate the checklist review into our brief shift handover, so that the designated person knows they are responsible that day.
If we see repeated issues with triage documentation or escalation, we can address them in short refreshers using A3.

The routine sounds fine to me.
As long as we rotate who fills in the checklist and keep it quick, it should not slow us down too much.
I like the idea of using the results to decide small improvements rather than just collecting numbers.

I am ok with the plan.
It would help if we have a simple way to see who is responsible for the checklist each week, maybe a small rota in the shared folder.

Great, I will document D5 as:
- one A4 checklist per shift, sample of 5 patients
- rotating responsible person per shift
- 90 percent minimum compliance, with review and action if below for more than two days.
Next, we need to agree on D6: how incidents and improvement suggestions will be logged and reviewed.
My proposal for A6 and T12:
- All staff can enter incidents and suggestions directly into A6.
- Categories: data error, delay, escalation issue, patient complaint, improvement idea, other.
- Mandatory fields: date, time, brief description, category, immediate action taken (if any).
- Review: twice-weekly short review in this channel, where we look at new entries and agree on owners for follow-up.
Please share if this workflow is clear and realistic, or if you prefer a different review frequency or ownership model.

The proposal for D6 makes sense to me.
Twice-weekly reviews feel like a good balance: frequent enough to act quickly, but not too heavy.
For ownership, I suggest that for each entry in A6 we assign a follow-up owner based on the area:
- reception-related issues: one of the administrative assistants
- nursing or clinical issues: 313168 or a delegate
- cross-cutting or system issues: we can escalate to operations or IT as needed.

I agree with the logging structure and categories in A6.
For nursing-related entries, I can take responsibility for initial review and either handle them directly or bring them to the head nurse if they require broader action.
Twice-weekly reviews are fine; we can align them with our existing brief clinical review slots.

For training, I will include a short exercise where staff practice entering a couple of sample incidents and improvement ideas into A6, so they are comfortable with the template from day one.
This should support the D6 workflow and make sure entries are clear and useful.

The logging process sounds straightforward.
It will be helpful to see patterns over time, especially for delays at reception.
I just ask that we keep the description field short so it does not take too long to fill in during busy times.

I am ok with the plan.
Maybe during the first week we can remind people in the daily check-in to add any incidents or ideas they noticed, so we get used to using A6.

Thanks for the input.
I will finalise D6 as:
- A6 used by all staff to log incidents and improvement ideas with the defined categories and mandatory fields.
- Twice-weekly short review in this channel to assign owners and agree on follow-up.
- Ownership by area as suggested: reception, nursing, and cross-cutting issues.
I will also update T9 and T12 to reflect these routines and make sure they are included in the SOP later.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training, communication, and pilot rollout details.

messages.text:
I have prepared initial drafts for:
- staff training deck and quick-reference sheets in A5 (for T5)
- an outline of the SOP in A7 (for T10)
- patient-facing communication text and poster layout in A8 (for T11).
For training (A5), there are separate sections for reception and nursing, plus a short part on using A4 and A6.
For the SOP (A7), I have structured it around the future workflow in A1, with links to A2, A3, A4, and A6.
For patient communication (A8), there is a short text in two languages explaining:
- what patients should bring
- what will happen at check-in and triage
- why we may ask them to arrive a bit earlier.
Please review and share feedback, especially on:
1) Training format and length.
2) Any missing or unclear steps in the SOP outline.
3) Whether the patient text is clear and not too long.

On A5 and training format:
- The split between reception and nursing content works well.
- The proposed 45-minute sessions might be hard to fit into some shifts.
Could we aim for two shorter modules of about 25 minutes each, so we can slot them before or after shift changes?
On A7, the SOP outline looks logical. I suggest adding a short section on exceptions, for example what to do if the EHR is down or if there is a sudden surge of patients.

For nursing training in A5:
- The triage scenarios are useful; I would add one or two borderline cases where the triage level is not obvious, to stimulate discussion.
- We should emphasise how to document triage level and escalation in the EHR, linking back to A3 and T3.
On A7, I agree with adding an exceptions section, including how to handle urgent cases when reception is overloaded.
For A8, the patient text is clear, but we might want to mention that patients can ask for help if they have difficulty reading or completing forms.

From reception, the quick-reference sheet in A5 is very helpful.
It clearly lists the steps and mandatory fields.
For training, shorter sessions would be easier to attend, as 196511 mentioned.
On A8, the patient text is understandable. Maybe we can add a simple line asking patients to have their ID and insurance card ready when they arrive, to speed things up.

I like that the training slides show screenshots of the EHR steps.
It makes it easier to follow.
I agree that shorter sessions would be better, especially for those of us who cover the phones.
The patient poster in A8 looks clear; big fonts and simple icons help.

From a quality perspective:
- A5 includes a good overview of A4 and A6; I will add one slide with the D5 and D6 routines so everyone understands the expectations.
- A7 should explicitly reference the daily QC checklist and incident log as part of the standard process, not as optional extras.
For A8, we should ensure that the patient text does not promise shorter waiting times immediately, but rather explains that the new process is designed to improve safety and organisation.

Thanks for the feedback.
I will adjust A5 to:
- split training into two 25-minute modules per group
- add more triage scenarios, including borderline cases
- include a slide summarising D5 and D6 routines.
I will also update A7 with an exceptions section and make sure A4 and A6 are clearly referenced as part of the standard process.
For A8, I will add the suggestions about ID and insurance cards, and clarify that the new process aims to improve safety and organisation rather than promising immediate shorter waits.

Next, we should confirm D7: training schedule, format, and which materials are mandatory for each role.
Proposal:
Format:
- Two 25-minute live sessions per group (reception and nursing), plus access to A5 and quick-reference sheets.
- Optional short recorded overview for those who cannot attend live.
Mandatory materials:
- Reception: sections on new workflow (A1), intake forms (A2), EHR sequence (T6), QC checklist (A4), and incident log (A6).
- Nursing: sections on triage protocol (A3), EHR documentation, escalation, QC checklist (A4), and incident log (A6).
Schedule (T7):
- Sessions spread over three days to cover all shifts, with at least one early and one late slot.
Please confirm if this works or suggest adjustments before we lock in D7 and start booking rooms and sending invites.

For nursing, the proposed D7 setup works.
I would like to ensure that at least one session per day is co-facilitated by someone from nursing, so that colleagues can ask practical questions.
We can also use part of the session to walk through A3 and a couple of real cases from recent weeks.

For reception, the plan is fine.
It would help if the quick-reference sheets are printed and available at the desk before the first session, so we can follow along and keep them afterwards.

I agree with the plan.
Shorter sessions and printed quick guides will make it easier to remember the steps.

From quality, I support D7 as proposed.
Please make sure that the parts on A4 and A6 are clearly marked as mandatory for all staff, since they are central to our monitoring approach.
I can join one session per group to answer questions on audits and incident logging.

I will adjust T5 and T7 to reflect D7:
- two 25-minute sessions per group
- co-facilitation with nursing for at least one nursing session per day
- printed quick-reference sheets ready in advance.
I will also prepare a short recorded overview for those who cannot attend live and share the link in this channel.

With the feedback incorporated, I will consider D7 confirmed and start drafting the detailed training schedule in T7.
Next, we need to agree on D8: pilot start date, scope, and patient communication channels.
Proposal:
- Pilot start: align with the next scheduled EHR maintenance window plus two days, to allow for any system changes and checks.
- Scope: all outpatient check-ins and triage during morning and afternoon shifts for one week; evening shift continues with the current process but logs incidents in A6.
- Patient communication channels: posters and leaflets (A8) at reception and waiting areas, short script for staff, and a brief note on the clinic website.
Please share if this timing and scope are realistic, and if we should adjust which shifts are included in the pilot.

The proposed pilot timing works from a nursing perspective, as long as we confirm staff availability for on-site support during the first two days.
Including morning and afternoon shifts is important, since that is when we see the highest volume.
I suggest we also include at least one evening shift mid-week in the pilot, so we can see how the process works with reduced staffing.

From reception, I agree with starting after the EHR maintenance window.
Including at least one evening shift in the pilot is a good idea, as 313168 said, because our staffing and patient mix are different then.
For patient communication, posters and a short script should be enough; many patients do not check the website before coming.

I am comfortable with the plan.
It would help if we know exactly which day we start so we can remind frequent patients who come often.
Also, having someone available on-site to answer questions during the first days will be reassuring.

From quality, I support aligning the pilot with the EHR maintenance window.
We should confirm with IT that there are no conflicting changes planned.
For D8, I suggest we:
- run the pilot for one full week including at least one evening shift
- use A6 actively during the pilot to capture incidents and improvement ideas
- schedule a short daily check-in in this channel to review any critical issues.
Patient communication via posters, leaflets, and staff script is sufficient; the website note is a nice addition but not essential for day one.

I will adjust A8 and T11 so that the patient text and posters are ready at least two days before the pilot start.
